title: Printing and Comments
intro: `print()` can show several values at once and lets you choose what goes between them and at the end. **Comments** are notes for humans: Python skips them completely.

questions.prompt: Separate values with commas and `print()` puts a space between them. Add `sep=` to choose a different separator. Add `end=` to change what goes at the end of the line — normally a new line.
questions.exampleCode:
print("Total:", 12)
print(2026, 10, 28, sep="-")
print("Loading", end="...")
print("done")
questions.explanation: `sep` goes *between* values; `end` goes *after* the last one.

questions.prompt: Print `Score: 42` by giving `print()` two values: the text `"Score:"` and the number `42`.

tests.name: output
tests.code: assert __output__.strip() == 'Score: 42', 'The output should be exactly: Score: 42'

questions.hint: Put a comma between the two values. `print()` adds the space for you.
questions.explanation: Commas let you mix text and numbers in one `print()`.

questions.hint: `sep` is placed between each pair of values.
questions.explanation: The separator ` > ` replaces the usual single space.

questions.prompt: Print the date `28/10/2026` from the three numbers `28`, `10` and `2026`, using `sep`.

tests.name: output
tests.code: assert __output__.strip() == '28/10/2026', 'The output should be exactly 28/10/2026 — no spaces.'

questions.explanation: Changing `sep` swaps every space between values for a slash.

questions.prompt: What does this print? (It's one line.)
questions.hint: `end=""` means nothing is added at the end, so the next `print()` continues on the same line.
questions.explanation: The first two calls end with nothing instead of a new line, so all three pieces join up.

questions.prompt: The first line is a note for humans, but Python tries to run it and fails. Turn it into a comment.
questions.starterCode:
Packing list for the weekend
print("passport")
print("charger")
questions.solution:
# Packing list for the weekend
print("passport")
print("charger")

tests.name: output
tests.code: assert __output__.split() == ['passport', 'charger'], 'The program should print passport and charger.'
tests.message: The program should print passport and charger.

questions.hint: A comment starts with `#`. Python ignores everything after it on that line.
questions.explanation: `#` turns the line into a note, so Python no longer tries to understand it.

questions.prompt:
What does Python do with this line?

```
# print("Hello")
```
questions.hint: Look at the very first character.
questions.explanation: Everything after `#` is a comment, even code. Commenting out a line is a handy way to switch it off.

questions.prompt: A **docstring** is a text in triple quotes on the very first line. It describes what the program does. Start the program with the docstring `"""Prints a weekly plan."""`, then print `Mon: swim`.

tests.name: docstring
tests.code: assert __doc__ is not None and __doc__.strip() == 'Prints a weekly plan.', 'The first line should be the docstring """Prints a weekly plan."""'
tests.message: Add the docstring as the very first line.

tests.name: output
tests.code: assert __output__.strip() == 'Mon: swim', 'The program should still print Mon: swim.'

questions.hint: Triple quotes look like `"""text"""`. It must be the first statement in the program.
questions.explanation: Python stores a program's first string as its docstring. Tools and other programmers read it to see what the code is for.

questions.prompt: Fill in the separator so each meal is printed on its own line.

tests.name: lines
tests.code: assert __output__.strip().splitlines() == ['Breakfast', 'Lunch', 'Dinner'], 'Each meal should be on its own line.'
tests.message: Each meal should be on its own line.

questions.hint: A new line is written `"\n"` inside quotes.
questions.explanation: `"\n"` is the new-line character, so each value starts a fresh line.

questions.prompt: Print `Countdown: 3 2 1 Go!` using **one** `print()` with five values: `"Countdown:"`, `3`, `2`, `1` and `"Go!"`. Add a comment above it saying what it does.

tests.name: output
tests.code: assert __output__.strip() == 'Countdown: 3 2 1 Go!', 'The output should be exactly: Countdown: 3 2 1 Go!'
tests.message: The output should be: Countdown: 3 2 1 Go!

questions.hint: Separate all five values with commas. The default separator is a space.
questions.explanation: One `print()` with several values is tidier than joining them by hand.
